title: Latency-aware queueing and tenant burst allocator (PRD - draft)
content:
Overview:
This doc proposes a latency-aware request queuing layer plus a tenant burst allocator for Dedicated pools. The design aims to let latency-sensitive tenants temporarily consume spare capacity without violating SLOs for other tenants, and to ensure graceful degradation when capacity is constrained.

Why this is different: we are intentionally combining a probabilistic, time-windowed queueing model (to absorb microbursts) with a short-lived lease system (burst allocator) that stitches available headroom across GPUs. This is not a pure credit ledger or strict quota; it is an adaptive, latency-first mechanism that prioritizes SLOs while enabling higher effective utilization.

Problem statement:
- Customers on Dedicated report two competing needs: (1) predictable latency for core traffic, and (2) occasional high-throughput bursts for batch jobs or sudden feature traffic.
- Current approaches (hard isolation or coarse burst credits) either leave GPU headroom unused or cause harmful tail-latency spikes when spikes coincide.
- We need a mechanism that provides soft isolation, measurable fairness, and bounded tail-latency for SLO-bound tenants.

Goals (success criteria):
- Maintain 99th-percentile latency SLOs for tenants with latency SLAs under typical burst scenarios (99% of observed bursts)
- Allow opportunistic bursts up to configurable headroom without manual reserve changes
- Provide clear observability: per-tenant burst allocations, queue depth, wait-time histograms, and eviction/reclaim events
- Operate safely across heterogeneous GPU pools and across region fallbacks

Non-goals:
- This is not a long-term replacement for reserved capacity contracts. Reserved capacity with committed units remains the path for sustained high-throughput needs.
- Not addressing model-level degradations (e.g., large context leading to KV cache miss amplification) — though we will surface signals to runtime teams.

User stories:
- As a developer on an e-commerce search team, I want short bursts for peak traffic during flash sales without provisioning more reserved capacity, while preserving 99th latency for search queries.
- As an infra SRE, I want to be able to inspect which tenants are being burst-allocated so I can analyze cost/latency tradeoffs.
- As an account manager, I want to define per-tenant burst caps and priority lanes for customers on gold plans.

High-level design:
1) Latency-aware queueing layer (front of Dedicated pool):
   - Requests are classified by tenant and latency sensitivity (derived from route/model tags).
   - Each class has a small, fast in-memory queue with a target wait-time bound (configurable per class).
   - Queue admission is probabilistic under overload: when an incoming request would exceed target wait-time, the classifier evaluates a short degradation path: redirect to cached response, fallback model, or return fast error depending on policy.
   - A dequeue scheduler prioritizes oldest requests subject to per-tenant fair-share weight and SLA priority.

2) Tenant burst allocator (short-lived leases):
   - Leases represent time-bounded invoices for extra GPU tokens (fractional GPU vcores or worker slots) that can be granted for a tenant to burst above base allocation for up to lease_duration (e.g., 30s to 5min).
   - Leases are minted by the allocator when spare capacity exists across the pool and lending that capacity does not threaten SLOs per predictive model.
   - Each lease includes an isolation label (soft/strict) and reclaim score; soft leases can be preempted earlier with gentle degradation, strict leases are only reclaimed if SLOs are at risk.

Key mechanisms and heuristics:
- Predictive headroom evaluation: use a rolling 60s forecast of arriving QPS and token burn to estimate safe lendable capacity. Models are conservative at pool-level and tenant-level.
- Latency budget scoring: each tenant has a latency budget metric (based on historical tail latency relative to SLO). The allocator reduces lending to tenants whose budget is low.
- Weighted fair-share with priority lanes: multi-tenant fairness is achieved by weighted queueing; higher-tier customers get wider burst lanes and higher priority for lease granting.
- Soft isolation via degradation policies: when a soft lease is reclaimed, the system attempts degradation actions in order: (1) fallback model call, (2) prefix cache hit, (3) adjust temperature/response length, (4) return 429-like response. Policies are configurable per route.

Data model (simple):
- Lease record fields (exposed in observability): lease_id, tenant_id, pool_id, tokens_granted, lease_start, lease_end, isolation_label, reclaim_score, source_signal (predictive headroom id).
- Queue metrics: queue_depth_by_tenant, median_wait_ms, p95_wait_ms, admission_reject_rate.

Operator UX and Controls:
- Console knobs: global burst enable, per-pool headroom % cap, per-tenant max_concurrent_leases, priority lane mapping.
- Auditable events in logs and audit trail for lease grants and reclaim reasons.
- Simulation mode: run allocator in “observe” mode where it records what it would have done without actually granting leases. Useful for ops validation before rollout.

Telemetry and SLOs to monitor:
- 99th token generation latency (by tenant, by route)
- Lease grant rate and average lease size
- Reclaim events and reason codes
- Admission reject rate from queue layer
- Effective GPU utilization and wasted headroom

Compatibility and constraints:
- Must integrate with serving runtime to understand KV cache impacts and per-request cost estimates.
- Should work with heterogeneous workers; allocator must convert tokens to worker slots in a normalized fashion.
- Considerations for model families: some models have cold-start or warmup behaviors that make short leases ineffective; these should be excluded via model metadata.

Rollout plan (staged):
- Phase 0 (sim): 4 weeks — run allocator in observe mode on a dedicated staging pool, collect metrics and false-positive reclaim signals.
- Phase 1 (soft): 2 weeks — enable soft leases for a small percentage of production pools with non-critical tenants.
- Phase 2 (priority lanes): 3 weeks — enable priority lanes for a subset of customers (internal + pilot customers).
- Phase 3 (broad): progressive rollout with feature flags and auto rollback on SLO regressions.

Open questions / risks:
- How to accurately map lease tokens to heterogeneous GPU resources (NVIDIA A100 vs L sequences)? Need runtime calibration.
- Potential for gaming: tenants may queue artificially to get larger leases. Mitigation: penalize repeated appeals and use historical usage as part of score.
- Interaction with Dedicated reserved capacity commitments: ensure billing/chargeback matches perceived burst benefit.

Action items / next steps:
- (ENG) Prototype a predictive headroom estimator using 30/60/120s windows (owner: Jonah)
- (RUNTIME) Add lease accounting hooks and eviction callbacks to runtime (owner: Diego)
- (OBS) Define dashboards and alerting thresholds for p99 changes (owner: Lena)
- (PRODUCT) Draft console UI wireframes for per-tenant burst controls (owner: Samira)

Related links and references:
- DCD-1423 (internal concept note on tenant fairness)
- ENG-5121 (runtime lease API proto)
- Runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/1189
- Console stub: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/DED/pages/27431

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally a sketch-level PRD. Looking for feedback on: the lease duration sweet spot, acceptable conservatism for the predictive model, and how much of this should be user-configurable versus product-op defaults.
- Please comment inline or add direct notes to DCD-1423.
